cells.tense: Right now the scale sits in your hands and you can feel it without gripping.
cells.ask: Something ended here a while back. Sit with what that left behind and lift out the piece worth holding onto. Give it a spot in the open. Nothing else needs moving today.
cells.core:
There's an evening when the scale tips and your hands register it before your mind does. It isn't a verdict you reach. It's a rightness you can feel, and it beats any ledger you could keep. What you're holding is small and it's yours. Fairness that lives in a body moves at the speed of touch, not counting, and being private it needs no audience to be true. Some part of you has known when a room was owed for a long stretch, longer than you've had words for it.

Weighing what's owed against what's given, you can go back over something already finished and lift out the one thing it left worth keeping. Give that piece a place you'll pass. You aren't building the instrument. It's already in your hands.
cells.sheetLine: You know what's fair before you've thought it through.
cells.verb: weighing what is owed against what is given

cells.tense: Soon the scale will tip somewhere you cannot see yet and you will brace for it.
cells.act: give a concrete piece of help and finish it
cells.ask: Take one person near you who's short on something. Do a real hand's worth for them, then close it — no total kept on the other side.
cells.core:
You're already in tomorrow's reckoning, running totals for things that haven't happened. The scale gets watched so hard it tips before anything lands on it. Feels like care. From the other side of a table it reads like bracing, and the counting carries even when you say nothing. What's owed here gets settled in the hand, not the head. Fairness in a body runs on contact, not on keeping books balanced before the books exist.

Give one real hand and close it the moment the hand is done, and you'll have a clean exchange to set beside the imagined ones. The tally doesn't have to go anywhere forever. It just sits one transaction out and watches whether the sky holds. It will, and you'll have a case on file.
cells.sheetLine: You feel the tilt before there's anything to weigh.
cells.verb: weighing what is owed against what is given

cells.tense: Something in you kept the accounting open long past the day it was settled.
cells.act: show someone the way you found
cells.ask: There's something you got through. Walk one person who's in it now along the turns that worked for you, then fall quiet and leave the rest to them.
cells.core:
The scale stands where you left it, untouched. You don't weigh what you owe anymore, and you don't ask what's owed back. What you keep noticing is what other people are being shorted. The felt sense of fairness hasn't left. It's aimed outward and away from you. Our record doesn't say what emptied the place it used to sit in, only that the spot is thin and it's still yours. That's not a flaw in your character. It's a scale waiting for weight, and it will take weight again.

Walking one person along the turns that worked for you is the same fairness, with your own name on it. You don't have to know why the ledger closed. Do this for someone facing what you got through, and stop when you've said the last turn.
cells.sheetLine: You notice what others are owed. Not what you are.
cells.verb: weighing what is owed against what is given

cells.tense: You are already weighing what is fair here — the pen is moving without your hand.
cells.act: distinguish what is yours from what you borrowed
cells.ask: Keep a page of everything asking something of you. Go down the list and mark which entries started with you and which came in from somewhere else. Keep the page. Decide nothing from it yet.
cells.core:
You're quietly the one who knows what's fair in this room, and if someone asked how, you'd say you followed the feeling. That knowing got separated from you, filed under the situation, kept off the record. What you do with fairness is real work. It steers the room, and the credit isn't coming back to you. The split is old and it isn't the whole truth of where you are.

Marking each pull mine or not mine puts your handwriting back on them. Set down what's asking something of you, note by each line whether it started here, and leave the page where you'll come across it again. Your own name will be on more of them than you believed.
cells.sheetLine: You are already weighing it — you just aren't signing it.
cells.verb: weighing what is owed against what is given

attempts.check: The record does not say how long the scale has been out of true, how it got there, or who was involved — so no cell dates the tipping or names what caused it. A reader might object that a private moral sense had its reasons all along, and this draft treats it as bent rather than broken or justified; that holds. The asks stay useful even if the read is off: each is a small act of touching the scale itself, and someone who disagrees can still do it. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any line about spilling being the person's own fault or about the reckoning already written — that flatters the reading, not the person, so it is gone.
